item.title: Putin holds 3-hour 'constructive' meeting with US envoys ahead of their Kyiv trip
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-06
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russian President Vladimir Putin (R) welcomes US special envoy Steve Witkoff (2nd L) and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner (L) prior to their talks in Moscow, Russia, September 5, 2026. /VCG
Russian President Vladimir Putin engaged in "constructive" talks lasting over three hours with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow on Saturday night, ahead of the delegation's visit to Kyiv on Sunday.
The diplomatic push comes as both Moscow and Kyiv said they would observe a temporary, three-day pause on capital airstrikes through Monday.
Putin had "substantive, constructive and extremely frank" talks with the US envoys "in a trusting atmosphere" at the Kremlin, with discussions on extremely serious issues taking place both in a working-format setting and informally over dinner, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said early Sunday morning. The conversation lasted three hours and 10 minutes.
Putin reaffirmed Russia's readiness to continue joint work with the United States in search of political and diplomatic solutions to the Ukrainian issue, Ushakov said.
Ushakov said that the Russian side provided clear and comprehensive assessments of the situation unfolding amid the special military operation.
"In particular, note was taken of the real advances made by the Russian army within the combat zone; confidence was expressed in achieving the stated objectives, and the need to eliminate all root causes of the conflict was emphasized," he noted.
The talks were not confined to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukraine crisis. Economic matters and potential large-scale, mutually beneficial Russian-US projects were also discussed in considerable detail, Ushakov said.
Overall, the negotiations can be described as "timely and highly beneficial" for both sides, Ushakov said, adding that it was confirmed that the heads of state of the two countries would maintain personal contact going forward and that work through Witkoff and Kushner would continue.
Ushakov said that the US envoys pledged that during their upcoming contacts in Kyiv "tomorrow," they would relay observations and assessments they had received directly from the Russian president regarding efforts to reach a durable, peaceful settlement to the Ukraine conflict.
Ukraine says ready to observe ceasefire during negotiations
Ukraine is ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the Russian cities involved in the negotiation process, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday.
"From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow," Zelenskyy said on X after a phone conversation with Witkoff and Kushner.
Ukraine is expecting Russia to take similar steps regarding Kyiv, Zelenskyy said.
According to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency, Witkoff and Kushner plan to visit Kyiv on Sunday following their trip to Moscow.
Zelenskyy said on Thursday that he expected to meet the US envoys in the Ukrainian capital.
Putin has ordered a three-day halt to strikes against Kyiv, a move linked to preparations for contacts with the US envoys, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Saturday.
(With input from Xinhua)

item.title: China, Singapore launch joint maritime exercise
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-06
This photo taken on Sept. 5, 2026 shows a view of the opening ceremony of a joint maritime exercise between China and Singapore in Zhanjiang, south China's Guangdong Province. (Photo by Ge Hanqiang/Xinhua)
GUANGZHOU, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- A joint maritime exercise between China and Singapore opened Saturday in south China's Guangdong Province, marking the fifth such cooperation held by the two countries.
The opening ceremony was held at a naval port in Zhanjiang. The exercise, conducted in the waters and airspace around the city, features live-fire drills, replenishment-at-sea, and joint search-and-rescue operations.
Two warships participate in the exercise -- the Chinese guided-missile frigate Dali and Singapore's frigate RSS Steadfast.
The exercise aims to deepen mutual trust, strengthen practical cooperation, and enhance their ability to jointly safeguard regional peace and stability, according to China's Ministry of National Defense earlier this week.
According to the ministry, the exercise is conducted in two phases, covering in-port exchanges and at-sea drills. The two sides will exchange expertise on diving operations, submarine search and rescue, and underwater medicine, and conduct drills in communications, replenishment-at-sea, joint maritime strikes, and joint search and rescue.
Chinese military expert Zhang Junshe said the joint search-and-rescue drills have important practical significance, given the heavy maritime traffic and complex weather and sea conditions in the South China Sea.
Under the search-and-rescue zones designated by the International Maritime Organization, both China and Singapore have maritime rescue responsibilities in relevant waters of the South China Sea, which requires their naval forces to fulfill corresponding duties, Zhang said.
He also noted that live-fire exercises and replenishment-at-sea help enhance the two navies' combat capabilities.
China and Singapore held their first bilateral maritime exercise in 2015. Such joint exercises have become a regular part of military exchanges between the two countries in recent years. In May 2025, the Chinese Navy dispatched a guided-missile frigate and a mine countermeasure vessel to Singapore for a joint exercise.
In addition to regular joint maritime exercises with Singapore, China also carries out routine joint drills and training with neighboring countries including Thailand and Cambodia.
This photo taken on Sept. 5, 2026 shows a view of the opening ceremony of a joint maritime exercise between China and Singapore in Zhanjiang, south China's Guangdong Province. (Photo by Gu Xingnan/Xinhua)

item.title: China moves to create phone-free classrooms, help minors navigate digital age
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-06
Children holding smiling face props play a game at a kindergarten in Qinyang City, central China's Henan Province, May 7, 2026. (Photo by Zhang Xinyu/Xinhua)
BEIJING, Sept. 5 (Xinhua) -- For Ye Hui, the past summer break has been a digital tug-of-war.
Every time she confiscated the tablet, her 10-year-old son found a way to crack the password. So when the new semester began, she finally felt relief -- not just because he was back in class, but because the law was now on her side.
"Teachers will be more persuasive, given that the ban on smart devices is no longer just a school policy," said Ye, who lives in southwest China's Chongqing municipality.
The ban Ye spoke of is stipulated in a local law on minor crime prevention, which took effect on Sept. 1. It prohibited Ye's son and his counterparts from bringing phones, tablets and other smart devices into school.
Official statistics showed that China has close to 200 million underage internet users, with over 97 percent of minors having online access.
Minors' attention being eroded by the algorithm is a problem faced by countries across the world in the digital age, said Wang Peng, a deputy research fellow at the Beijing Academy of Social Sciences.
Putting a mobile device school ban into law is necessary, as it provides legal support for schools to enforce the ban to keep students from such erosion, Wang said.
Chongqing is the latest to elevate a phone ban from a school policy to legislation, as the entire country is working to build a safe and healthy internet environment for children's wholesome growth.
A similar legal ban has already been put in place in Guangzhou in Guangdong Province, Zhengzhou in Henan Province and places across Fujian Province.
The aim is better prevention of internet addiction among underage students, according to Chongqing municipal legislature, noting the provision cited a 2021 guidance document on the protection of minors' rights and interests in school by the Ministry of Education.
In mulling over the local law on minor crime prevention, Chongqing's legislative body found that exposure to bad information as a result of smartphone usage caused some school-age children to develop unhealthy ideas and values, and even commit crimes.
Ye was one of the worrying parents struggling to keep their children away from smartphones' bad influence. Her son spent nearly eight hours every day on screen and even paid for virtual skins and props for online games during the past summer vacation. "He could always find a way to unlock the tablet."
Strict restrictions on smart device use could help nip internet addiction in the bud, Ye hoped.
Xiao Junyi, a student from the 29th Middle School in Chongqing, welcomed the phone ban in school, admitting phones had proven detrimental to students' level of concentration and undermined their learning.
"We would secretly take out the phone and surf online when class was on," Xiao said.
Teachers believe when the phone ban becomes a law provision, it will be more convincing to students and easier for them to enforce.
"It will save a lot of unnecessary lecturing," said Hu Ranrui'an, a deputy head teacher at the Science City Middle School Affiliated to Chongqing Normal University.
But in reality, some children, particularly middle school students who have no parent to take them from and to school, do need cell phones for emergency contact.
"It's not a one-size-fits-all ban," said Jiang Yongsong, a supervisor from the 29th Middle School. There is a provision in the law that allows parents to file a written application if students need phones in school, he said.
Countries around the world have also been introducing bans, with smartphones increasingly seen as a source of classroom distraction and a potential threat to students' well-being.
UNESCO's latest Global Education Monitoring Report showed that 114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58 percent of countries worldwide.
However, experts cautioned that restriction is not enough to address the problem, calling for joint efforts from society, school and family.
After physically isolating minors from the digital world, there will be room for efforts to foster their concentration and capabilities for in-depth and critical thinking, said Wang Peng.
Ye Hui has already mapped out the reclaimed hours from the screen -- board games on Mondays, jogging on Wednesdays and weekend hikes to replace the virtual battles. "It's about proving the real world can win the battle for his attention," she said.

item.title: International experts explain rescue challenges at mudslide-hit China-Nepal border
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-06
Over a week after a catastrophic mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on August 26, search and rescue operations there have kicked into higher gear.
Chinese rescue teams fully reopened the only land route to Gyirong Port on Wednesday morning after overcoming challenges such as damaged roads, rugged terrain and other obstacles, allowing rescuers, relief supplies, equipment and heavy machinery to reach the core disaster area by road to carry out more intensive rescue operations.
Rescuers still face difficult conditions in the disaster area, with teams deploying ground radar and aerial surveys to monitor slope deformation and other potential secondary disasters and help ensure the safety of search and rescue operations.
Rescue personnel conduct search and rescue operations in the disaster-hit area of Gyirong Port, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, September 2, 2026. /VCG
Against such complex and volatile disaster conditions, international disaster management experts have highlighted the unprecedented difficulties of the ongoing border rescue operations while acknowledging China's robust emergency response capacity.
Akhilesh Surjan, a specialist in humanitarian and disaster emergency management at Australia's Charles Darwin University, stressed the necessity of sustained, meticulous search efforts amid lingering uncertainties.
In highly complex cascading catastrophes like this cross-border glacial mudslide, life-search operations must continue as long as credible survival possibilities remain, Surjan said, adding that the absence of survivors in one spot cannot rule out survival chances in other buried areas.
"Every search decision carries profound humanitarian and diplomatic implications for cross-border disaster relief," Surjan told The Straits Times.
Winston Chang, former global lead of the UN International Search and Rescue Advisory Group, pointed out that the unique geological aftermath of glacial mudslides creates enormous operational hurdles, even for well-equipped rescue forces such as China's.
Powerful glacial mudslides can sweep buildings and debris several kilometers downstream, completely altering the original terrain. Rescuers face great uncertainty over what lies beneath layers of deep, fluid mud and mixed rock fragments, Chang explained.
He added that the unstable terrain creates a "logistical nightmare" for on-site operations.
Specialized safety equipment, including fixed anchor points and safety ropes, is mandatory for every forward movement, he said, stressing that safety management stands as the top priority throughout the entire rescue process.
People commute across the Trishuli River via an installed zip line in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli Center in Nepal's Nuwakot district, September 4, 2026. /VCG
Echoing the view, Surjan noted that the ongoing rainfall, poor visibility, fragile mountain slopes and frequent secondary geological hazards constitute compound risks that threaten rescue personnel and slow down operational progress.
Beyond on-site rescue difficulties, the rare, sudden nature of high-altitude glacial disasters also exposes systemic gaps in global early warning systems, according to newly published research.
An article published in Nature on Wednesday highlighted the urgent need to upgrade future monitoring and forecasting systems.
The disaster proved difficult to predict because it was triggered by the sudden failure of a high-altitude glacier-rock system rather than typical signals, such as extreme rainfall or rising glacial lakes, according to the article.
Manoochehr Shirzaei, a geophysicist at Virginia Tech, emphasized the limitations of traditional ground-monitoring technologies in tackling emerging climate-driven geological risks.
Conventional monitoring systems fail to detect early signs of high-altitude glacial-rock slope instability. There is an urgent demand for integrated, space-based observation networks to fill the gap, Shirzaei told Nature.
The Nature study further proposed a systematic solution, "What is still largely missing is a regional satellite-based system that routinely searches for accelerating glacier and rock-slope deformation and then connects that information directly to downstream flood and avalanche modeling."

item.title: Xi's cultural journey through museums
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-05
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, accompanied by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his wife Entissar El-Sisi, tour the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, Egypt, Sept. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
CAIRO, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- On the Giza Plateau, the majestic pyramids, silent witnesses to millennia of history, now gaze across at the Grand Egyptian Museum.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, visited the museum on Wednesday during his state visit to Egypt, where they were warmly received by Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and his wife.
Surrounded by ancient artifacts, the two presidential couples toured the grand galleries, posing for a photo before a towering statue of Ramses II, one of the most famous pharaohs of Egypt, as curators delivered a swift primer on pharaonic history.
"This museum is a book with endless pages," Xi said.
He, during the tour, also urged the two countries to promote the inclusive coexistence and mutual learning among different civilizations, and pool greater strength from civilizations to advance the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.
As the world's largest museum dedicated to a single civilization, the Grand Egyptian Museum houses more than 100,000 precious artifacts. Locals have newly dubbed it the "fourth pyramid of Giza."
This photo taken on Nov. 4, 2025 shows a golden mask at the King Tutankhamun exhibition hall of the Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza, Egypt. (Xinhua/Ahmed Gomaa)
The Grand Egyptian Museum is just one of the many museums Xi has visited over the years. Whether on domestic inspection tours or overseas trips, his visits have taken him to the Sanxingdui Museum in southwest China's Sichuan province and the Yinxu Museum in central China's Henan province, key sites of early Chinese civilization, as well as the Amir Timur Museum in Uzbekistan, and the ancient Maya ruins of Chichen Itza in Mexico. The list goes on.
Such frequent museum visits stem from Xi's longstanding emphasis on preserving and carrying forward traditional culture. For Xi, museums are important places that protect and pass on human civilizations.
In November 2019, during his visit to the Acropolis Museum in Athens, Greece, Xi paused to admire the relief of the "Pensive Athena," the Greek goddess of war and wisdom. He and then Greek President Prokopis Pavlopoulos explored how ancient Chinese and Greek civilizations expressed their reflections on war and their shared longing for peace.
Museums have also been a frequent choice for Xi to present traditional Chinese culture when hosting foreign dignitaries.
Tourists visit the Palace Museum, also known as the Forbidden City, in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 29, 2023. (Xinhua/Li Xin)
During U.S. President Donald Trump's two visits to China in 2017 and 2026, Xi hosted him at the Forbidden City, or the Palace Museum, and the Temple of Heaven, respectively, using the historic sites to illustrate the Chinese philosophy of pursuing peace and harmony.
In Xi's eyes, museums are not simply repositories of the past. They offer people a chance to discover unfamiliar histories, recognize common threads of human creativity and gain a deeper understanding of one another.
During his first state visit to Egypt in 2016, Xi toured Luxor, a city widely known as one of the world's largest open-air museums. Walking along the main avenue of Luxor Temple, Xi and Sisi discussed the distinctive features of their two ancient civilizations, recalling their long history of exchanges and mutual learning. At the temple, they also witnessed the launch of the 2016 China-Egypt Culture Year, a landmark moment in bilateral cultural exchanges.
Today, the Grand Egyptian Museum provides a new setting for that dialogue between the two ancient civilizations. In a message to Sisi on its opening last year, Xi said that the museum will leave a profound mark on Egypt's cultural history and play an important role in preserving and passing on the ancient Egyptian civilization.
It is encouraging to see the two ancient civilizations reaching out to each other, with the two peoples growing ever closer through mutual understanding and affinity, Xi said in the message.
From Beijing to Cairo, Xi's museum visits underscore how history can bridge rather than divide civilizations, enabling them to deepen mutual understanding and draw on the wisdom of the past to shape the road ahead.
As Xi has observed, "Museums bridge the past, present, and future."

item.title: Xi's Kyrgyzstan visit promotes permanent good-neighborliness, friendship, says Chinese FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Kyrgyzstan has strengthened the bonds of permanent good-neighborliness and friendship between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.
It has also opened up new prospects for shared prosperity, deepened commitment to a shared future and demonstrated China's principle of amity, sincerity, mutual benefit and inclusiveness in its neighborhood diplomacy, he noted.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks while briefing reporters on the conclusion of Xi's attendance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit in Bishkek and state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt from August 30 to September 3.
The visit to the Central Asian nation came as China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation has ushered in a "golden period" of rapid development, as noted by Xi in a written speech delivered upon his arrival, with the two countries working to translate their longstanding friendship and strong political mutual trust into broader cooperation and greater benefits for their people.
During the Kyrgyz leg of the trip, the two sides signed more than 30 cooperation documents covering trade, transportation, science and technology, education, cultural and people-to-people exchanges, among other areas.
The most significant political outcome was the signing of a treaty on permanent good-neighborliness, friendship and cooperation by the two heads of state, legally cementing their commitment to everlasting friendship, Wang said.
The treaty marks a new level of political mutual trust, mutual support and strategic coordination while opening broader avenues for future relations, he noted.
The two heads of state also agreed to elevate practical cooperation, with high-quality Belt and Road cooperation as the main focus, consolidating trade and investment, connectivity and green minerals cooperation while expanding into emerging fields such as the digital economy, clean energy and artificial intelligence, Wang added.
Xi, during his talks with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, said the two sides should ensure the high-quality construction of the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, calling it a major transportation artery that carries the development aspirations of the people across the region.
Japarov, for his part, said Kyrgyzstan stands ready to actively advance the construction of the railway project so as to turn it into a "steel Silk Road" for the new era and a new bond of friendship between the two countries.

item.title: Xi's four-point proposal offers Chinese solution for Mideast peace, stability, says Chinese FM
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-04
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, in Cairo, Egypt, September 2, 2026. /Xinhua
Chinese President Xi Jinping's four-point proposal on building a new security architecture in the Middle East once again offers a Chinese solution for achieving long-term peace and stability in the region, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks while briefing reporters on the conclusion of Xi's attendance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Bishkek Summit and state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt.
Xi put forward the proposal in his talks with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi, calling for unleashing internal drivers, advancing an integrated approach, cementing development foundation, and enhancing international coordination.
International observers believe that Xi's proposal has offered a viable path toward resolving the Middle East's security dilemma, Wang said.
During the visit, Xi had in-depth exchanges with leaders of various countries on world affairs and hotspot issues, speaking up for peace and standing up for justice, said Wang.
On the sidelines of the Bishkek summit, Xi held separate meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Mongolian President Ukhnaa Khurelsukh.
Xi and Putin agreed to deepen China-Russia comprehensive strategic coordination, advance reform of global governance, promote a multipolar world, and jointly safeguard world peace, stability and development, Wang noted.
Guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Diplomacy, China has been exploring a distinctly Chinese approach to resolving hotspot issues, Wang said, adding that no matter how complex the disputes or how intense the conflicts, China will always stand firmly on the side of peace and dialogue and on the right side of history.

item.title: Global resonance of Xi's selfless commitment to the people
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-03
Chinese President Xi Jinping holds talks with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, Aug. 31, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi)
On the morning of August 31, during talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov expressed admiration for the remarkable development achievements China has made under the leadership of Xi, and voiced willingness to learn from China's experience in state governance, particularly Xi's commitment to the people, as embodied in his words, "I will fully commit to the people and never fail them."
In March 2019, during his state visit to Italy, Xi met with Roberto Fico, then president of the Italian Chamber of Deputies.
Fico asked Xi, "What did you feel when you were elected Chinese president?"
"Governing such a huge country requires a strong sense of responsibility and hard work," said Xi. "For the good of my people, I will put aside my own well-being. I am willing to be selfless and devote myself to China's development."
Xi has spoken of this conviction on multiple occasions. During his trip to the United States in November, 2023, Xi recalled in a speech at a welcome dinner hosted by friendly organizations that, before turning 16, he was in a village in northern Shaanxi Province, where he lived and farmed with villagers, and knew about their worries and needs. He said that, over the past half-century, he had always felt confident and strong when staying with the people. “Serving the people selflessly and living up to their expectations is my lifelong commitment,” he said.
Xi not only keeps in mind major issues concerning the national economy and people's livelihood, but also cares about the everyday concerns of ordinary people.
During his local inspection tours, Xi chatted with local residents about their daily lives and household finances, felt the quilts on their beds to make sure they stay warm, lifted the lids of cooking pots to see whether they eat well, asked about whether they had rich cultural and spiritual lives, and attached great importance to the healthy development of young people.
From securing a decisive victory in poverty alleviation to comprehensively advancing rural revitalization, from achieving a moderately prosperous society in all respects to marching toward common prosperity, Chinese Communists in the new era have borne in mind the country's most fundamental interests — ensuring that the people live happy lives. They have devoted themselves wholeheartedly to this cause, forged ahead undauntedly to achieve it, and made persistent efforts to bring it to fruition.
People's well-being is of utmost importance in Chinese modernization. China's development achievements vividly demonstrate its people-centered development philosophy. China now has the world's largest education, social security and healthcare systems, while achieving historic strides in making education universally available. During the 14th Five-Year Plan period, average life expectancy in China rose to 79.25 years, more than 12 million new urban jobs were created each year on average, and direct settlement of cross-provincial medical expenses benefited 560 million medical visits nationwide.
In the opening year of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, China's head-of-state diplomacy has witnessed one highlight after another, with more and more foreign leaders seeking inspiration from China's governance model for their own development.
During his state visit to China, Mozambican President Daniel Francisco Chapo made a special trip to Banyan Village of Huzhu Tu Autonomous County in northwest China's Qinghai Province, where Xi Jinping visited during an inspection tour in 2016. "Seeing is believing. With China's targeted poverty alleviation policies effectively implemented, Banyan Village has undergone tremendous changes, which is truly inspiring." Chapo said, adding that the experience is also exemplary for the world.
At the entrance of Yucun Village in Anji County, east China’s Zhejiang Province, Thongloun Sisoulith, General Secretary of the Lao People's Revolutionary Party Central Committee and Lao President, took a photo of the inscription carved on a boulder, which reads, "lucid waters and lush mountains are invaluable assets." After hearing a briefing on the "Green Rural Revival Program" — which was initiated in June 2003 by Xi, then secretary of the CPC Zhejiang Provincial Committee, with a plan to renovate about 10,000 incorporated villages in five years and transform about 1,000 central villages among them into examples of moderate prosperity in all respects — Thongloun lauded the program as remarkable for creating countless beautiful villages.
During Xi’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, how to further improve people's well-being remains a key concern for him. "Pursuing high-quality cooperation on the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, a transportation artery carrying the region's aspirations for development," "further promoting personnel exchanges and strengthening cooperation in such areas as youth, media, tourism, sports, and medical care, and at subnational levels," and "steadily consolidating the societal foundation of and popular support for China-Kyrgyzstan friendship" — these are among the priorities highlighted by Xi.
"The people's aspiration for a better life is what we are striving for." This deep commitment to the people is reflected in practice, offers inspiration for the future, and allows the international community to gain a deeper appreciation of the CPC's people-centered governance philosophy and its strong sense of mission and responsibility.
"I will fully commit to the people and never fail them." This is not merely a powerful pledge, but a commitment translated into concrete action. The vision of enabling hundreds of millions of people to live better lives is resonating more widely around the world.

item.title: Pushing in by Land, Water and Air: Expert Explains Extreme Hurdles in Mudslide Rescue
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
A total of 2,141 rescue personnel have been mobilized for search and rescue operations after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. Rescue teams are advancing into the hardest-hit core area simultaneously by water, land and air. An expert explained mudslides like this occur under particular terrain and water conditions, and that creates several challenges for rescue teams.
